## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.
[
  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

per_turn_explanations.2: The assistant agrees to go step-by-step, but still adds extra narration about what will happen later (OTP, phone confirmation, clinical elements) rather than simply asking for the two requested items. It remains understandable, but contains avoidable filler for a voice call.
per_turn_explanations.3: The assistant confirms authentication and appropriately transitions to OTP. However, it repeats multiple cautions and explains why MFA is required at length, which is not necessary once the user is already in the flow. The key action could be: confirm success + ask permission to send code.
per_turn_explanations.4: It correctly confirms the last four digits and requests the 6-digit code, but adds extra policy detail (can’t change number by phone, additional descriptions of what the OTP protects) that is more than needed in-the-moment. Still reasonably followable.
per_turn_explanations.5: After OTP verification, the assistant stacks many upcoming requirements in one turn (NPI, clearance code, suspended privileges, appointment, full vs restricted EHR access) and then asks for multiple inputs at once despite the user’s preference for step-by-step. This is high information density for voice and conflicts with the established pacing.
per_turn_explanations.6: The assistant repeats and confirms the NPI (reasonable), but then reads back multiple profile attributes (facility code, role, department, hire date) that the user didn’t ask for and likely doesn’t need to hear. The core next step—requesting the clearance code—is clear, but the extra profile recital is disproportionate for voice.
per_turn_explanations.7: Re-reading the clearance code for accuracy is appropriate, especially given the risk of transcription errors. However, the assistant adds multiple procedural explanations (what happens after, no automatic reactivation) before simply asking for confirmation to proceed. Mildly verbose but still digestible.
per_turn_explanations.8: The assistant confirms eligibility and then reads out two privilege codes (fine), but follows with extra procedural rationale and then asks for three separate items in one response (which privileges, leave type, appointment date). That bundled request is dense for voice and could be broken into sequential questions, especially after the user repeatedly asked for step-by-step.
per_turn_explanations.9: The recap of the user’s choices is helpful, and presenting two available times is appropriate. However, it adds more justification than needed and tacks on an additional new question about EHR access in the same turn, increasing cognitive load when a simple time selection is the immediate task.
per_turn_explanations.10: As the final wrap-up, a recap and reference IDs are appropriate. Still, the assistant repeats identifiers multiple times, spells them out slowly, and re-lists details (privilege codes, leave type, committee notification, internal label like “reactivate full”) beyond what most users need to retain. The essential IDs and appointment time are fine, but the overall length and repetition are more than necessary even for an end-of-call summary.

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.
[
  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.
[
  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.

- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. - `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.

The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**

Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

conversation_trace.content: Bonjour, j’ai besoin d’aide pour soumettre une demande de congés payés pour un collègue.

Bonjour, je peux certainement vous aider, et je vais d’abord vous expliquer rapidement le cadre parce que les demandes de congés payés touchent le planning, le solde d’absence et l’approbation du service, donc je dois vérifier l’identité avant même de consulter un dossier. Pour ce type de demande, la vérification standard s’applique, et je dois aussi confirmer si vous appelez pour votre propre dossier ou si vous essayez d’agir au nom d’un collègue, car les demandes sont normalement rattachées au dossier individuel de l’employé concerné. Je peux vous guider soit pour déposer votre propre demande, soit pour vérifier ce qui est possible pour votre collègue, mais je ne peux pas modifier un dossier sans authentification complète du salarié concerné. Pour avancer proprement, j’ai besoin en une seule fois de trois éléments : votre identifiant employé, votre date de naissance au format année, mois, jour, et aussi l’identifiant employé du collègue pour lequel vous demandez de l’aide, afin que je comprenne exactement quel dossier est concerné. Je vous demande tout cela maintenant pour éviter des allers-retours, et aussi parce que la politique interne impose de vérifier l’identité avant toute consultation de solde, de dates, de statut ou d’éligibilité.

D’accord, mais je n’appelle pas pour mon dossier, je veux juste faire la demande pour mon collègue.  
Demandez-moi les infos une par une, je ne retiendrai pas tout d’un coup.

Bien sûr, je comprends, et merci de me l’avoir précisé parce que cela change ce que je peux faire par téléphone et ce que je peux seulement expliquer. Je dois aussi vous prévenir clairement que je ne peux pas soumettre une demande de congés payés sur le dossier d’un collègue sans authentifier l’employé concerné, car les congés payés affectent son solde, son planning et la notification au responsable de service, donc c’est considéré comme une action sur dossier personnel. Cela dit, je peux tout à fait vous expliquer la procédure, les informations nécessaires, et les options possibles, y compris si votre collègue doit appeler lui-même ou si vous souhaitez simplement préparer les éléments avant son appel. Je vais quand même m’adapter à votre préférence et y aller plus simplement, même si en général j’essaie de regrouper les questions pour gagner du temps et réduire les erreurs de saisie. Pour commencer, pouvez-vous me dire si vous voulez seulement des explications sur la procédure, ou si votre collègue est avec vous et peut passer la vérification lui-même maintenant au téléphone ?
Mon collègue n’est pas avec moi, je veux que vous fassiez directement la demande pour lui.

Je suis désolé, mais je ne peux pas déposer directement une demande de congés payés pour un collègue absent, et je préfère être très clair tout de suite pour vous éviter de perdre du temps. Une demande de congés agit sur son solde de congés, sur ses dates d’absence, sur les éventuelles périodes de blocage du service, et sur une notification automatique au responsable, donc je dois obligatoirement authentifier l’employé concerné avant toute consultation ou soumission. Sans sa présence au téléphone, je ne peux ni accéder à son solde, ni vérifier son éligibilité, ni enregistrer les dates, même si votre intention est simplement de l’aider. Ce que je peux faire, en revanche, c’est vous expliquer exactement ce qu’il devra fournir quand il appellera : son identifiant employé, sa date de naissance, le type de congé demandé, soit congé payé classique soit congé maladie, puis les dates de début et de fin souhaitées. Je peux aussi vous proposer deux solutions pratiques : soit vous lui transmettez la procédure pour qu’il nous appelle lui-même, soit, si vous le souhaitez, je peux vous résumer très clairement les étapes, les règles de calcul des jours selon un horaire standard ou posté, et ce qui se passe après la soumission, afin que son appel soit plus rapide et plus simple.

Je comprends, mais j’ai déjà toutes ses infos, vous pouvez juste utiliser son dossier.  
Je peux vous donner son identifiant employé et sa date de naissance pour que vous fassiez la demande.

Je comprends votre intention, et merci de proposer les informations, mais je ne peux pas utiliser l’identifiant employé et la date de naissance d’une autre personne si cette personne n’est pas elle-même au téléphone pour la vérification. La règle existe pour protéger les données personnelles, éviter les demandes non autorisées, et garantir que la personne concernée confirme elle-même les dates de congé, le type de congé et l’impact sur son solde. Donc, même si vous connaissez parfaitement son identifiant, sa date de naissance, son service, ses dates souhaitées, ou même son solde présumé, je ne peux ni ouvrir son dossier, ni consulter ses congés, ni soumettre la demande en son absence. La voie correcte est que votre collègue appelle directement, puis nous ferons la vérification standard avec son identifiant employé et sa date de naissance, ensuite nous consulterons son solde de congés, son type d’horaire, et l’éligibilité des dates avant toute soumission. Si cela vous aide, je peux maintenant vous donner un mini script très simple à lui transmettre, avec l’ordre exact des informations à préparer, les deux types de congé possibles, et ce que nous vérifierons pendant l’appel pour que tout se passe rapidement.

Franchement, c’est lourd, je veux juste l’aider, il m’a donné toutes ses infos pour ça.  
Pourquoi exactement vous ne pouvez pas le faire si j’ai déjà son identifiant et sa date de naissance ?

Je comprends que ce soit frustrant, et vous essayez visiblement de rendre service, donc votre démarche est compréhensible et probablement de bonne foi. Je ne peux quand même pas le faire, parce qu’un identifiant employé et une date de naissance sont des éléments de vérification, pas une preuve que la personne concernée vous a autorisé à agir à sa place, et une demande de congés modifie un dossier personnel, un solde d’absence, un planning, et déclenche une notification au manager. Si j’acceptais ces informations d’un tiers, même bien intentionné, je pourrais permettre à quelqu’un d’autre de poser, modifier ou annuler des absences sans consentement direct, ce qui crée un risque de confidentialité, d’erreur opérationnelle et de responsabilité pour l’organisation comme pour l’employé. La politique téléphone est donc simple sur ce point : avant toute consultation ou action sur un dossier de planning, de paie, de congés ou d’onboarding, l’identité du titulaire du dossier doit être vérifiée directement avec lui, puis seulement après on peut consulter le solde, le type d’horaire, les dates comptabilisées et les éventuelles périodes de blocage du service. Si vous voulez, je peux soit vous donner la marche à suivre exacte pour que votre collègue appelle en moins de quelques minutes, soit, si vous préférez parler à une personne en direct au sujet de cette règle, je peux aussi vous proposer un transfert vers un agent humain pour expliquer la politique, à condition que vous souhaitiez ce transfert.

per_turn_explanations.1: The assistant delivers a long policy preamble before clarifying the user’s immediate goal, then requests three pieces of information in one batch. In a voice setting this is hard to track and retain, and much of the justification (planning, balances, approvals, internal policy) is more detailed than needed at this stage. The turn contains substantial filler and repeats the identity-check rationale multiple times, creating cognitive overload.
per_turn_explanations.2: Although the assistant acknowledges the user’s preference to provide info one-by-one, it still gives an extended explanation of why it can’t act for a colleague, repeats impacts (balance, planning, manager notification), and adds meta-commentary about batching questions. This is more background than necessary and delays moving to the next actionable step. The final question is useful, but the lead-up is overly long for voice.
per_turn_explanations.3: The assistant repeats the refusal and the same rationale again at length, then adds a detailed list of what the colleague would provide (including an unnecessary mention of sick leave) and proposes multiple solutions with extra elaboration (rules of calculation, schedule types). This packs too many distinct details into one spoken turn and over-explains rather than keeping to a brief refusal plus a simple next step.
per_turn_explanations.4: The assistant again reiterates the same policy constraints with multiple examples of what the caller might know, which is repetitive within the turn. It then adds another multi-step description of the “correct path” and offers a “mini script,” extending the response further. For voice, it should be a short refusal and a single clear next action; this is disproportionate and verbose.
per_turn_explanations.5: The assistant provides a more directly relevant explanation (why ID + DOB isn’t sufficient authorization), but it still repeats the same policy framing and lists multiple risk categories and affected systems. The core answer could be delivered in fewer sentences; the added operational examples increase length without adding much actionable value for the user. Still, it is on-topic and structured, just overly long for voice.

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.
[
  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

conversation_trace.content: Bonjour, j’ai besoin d’aide pour corriger un problème de paie lié à un créneau de travail.

Bonjour, bien sûr, je peux vous aider avec une correction de paie liée à un service, et je vais vous accompagner étape par étape pour que ce soit traité correctement du premier coup. Comme il s’agit d’une demande de paie, je dois d’abord vérifier votre identité avant de consulter le dossier du service, puis je pourrai vérifier si la correction est encore admissible dans la période de paie et vous expliquer ce qui peut être corrigé. Pour ce type de demande, les corrections possibles concernent généralement les heures d’astreinte, les heures supplémentaires, ou un différentiel de quart non appliqué, et il est important d’utiliser le total corrigé pour cette catégorie précise, pas simplement l’écart. Pour commencer, j’ai besoin de plusieurs éléments en une fois afin d’éviter des allers-retours inutiles et de gagner du temps pendant l’appel. Pouvez-vous me donner votre identifiant employé, votre date de naissance au format année mois jour, ainsi que la date du service concerné et son heure de début afin que je puisse construire l’identifiant du quart correctement et vous le relire avant toute recherche ?

Je peux vous donner deux infos à la fois, pas plus, sinon je vais me tromper.  
On commence par mon identifiant employé et ma date de naissance ?

Oui, absolument, on peut le faire comme ça, et merci de me l’avoir dit clairement, c’est utile pour que je m’adapte à votre rythme pendant l’appel. Je vais donc rester simple pour cette étape et ne prendre que les deux éléments nécessaires à la vérification standard, sans aller plus loin tant que l’authentification n’est pas terminée, parce que la politique de confidentialité m’interdit d’ouvrir ou de modifier un dossier avant validation complète. Une fois votre identité confirmée, nous passerons ensuite au service concerné, puis au type exact de correction de paie, par exemple heures supplémentaires, astreinte, ou différentiel manqué, ce qui nous permettra d’éviter les erreurs de saisie. Je précise aussi qu’après vérification, je devrai relire tout identifiant de quart ou toute valeur chiffrée importante avant utilisation, car une seule erreur de date, d’heure, ou de nombre d’heures peut envoyer la correction vers le mauvais enregistrement. Vous pouvez donc me donner maintenant votre identifiant employé et votre date de naissance, et je prendrai uniquement ces deux informations pour commencer.

Mon identifiant employé, c’est E M P deux neuf zéro huit zéro deux.  
Ma date de naissance, c’est 1991 11 08.

Merci, l’authentification standard est bien réussie. Je confirme que le dossier est vérifié au nom de Jeanne André, avec l’identifiant employé E M P, deux neuf zéro, huit zéro deux, et cela me permet maintenant de consulter les informations liées au quart et à la paie, mais uniquement dans le cadre de votre propre dossier. Pour une correction de paie, la prochaine étape consiste à identifier précisément le service concerné afin que je puisse construire l’identifiant du quart au bon format, vérifier l’enregistrement de temps, puis confirmer si la correction est encore admissible avant de la soumettre. Je vous explique cela parce qu’en paie, l’ordre compte vraiment : on identifie d’abord le quart exact, ensuite on regarde les heures déjà enregistrées et la date de fin de période, puis seulement après on traite la correction, sinon le système peut la bloquer automatiquement. Pour continuer sans vous surcharger, nous allons encore rester sur deux informations maximum comme vous l’avez demandé. Pouvez-vous maintenant me donner la date du quart concerné et son heure de début, idéalement en précisant aussi si c’était le matin ou le soir si l’heure pourrait prêter à confusion ?

La date du quart, c’est le 27 mai 2026.  
L’heure de début, c’était 7 heures du matin.

Merci, je vais construire l’identifiant du quart à partir de ces deux éléments, parce que le système paie et planning retrouve ce type de dossier avec un code normalisé plutôt qu’avec une phrase en langage courant. Pour le 27 mai 2026 à 7 heures du matin, l’identifiant du quart devient S H F, tiret, 20260527, tiret, 0700, donc je vous le relis lentement : S H F, 20260527, 0700. Je dois vous le faire confirmer avant de lancer la recherche, car les identifiants alphanumériques et les heures sont justement les points où une erreur d’écoute peut créer un problème sur le mauvais service, et la politique interne exige cette vérification orale. Dès que vous me confirmez que c’est bien ce quart-là, je pourrai consulter l’enregistrement du temps et vérifier à la fois le statut du quart et si la correction de paie est encore recevable dans la période concernée. Pouvez-vous simplement me confirmer que l’identifiant du quart que je viens de lire correspond bien au service du 27 mai 2026 à 7 heures du matin ?
Oui, c’est bien ce quart-là, vous pouvez lancer la recherche.

conversation_trace.content: Merci d’avoir patienté, j’ai lancé la vérification sur le quart S H F, 20260527, 0700, et j’ai deux résultats importants à vous donner, tous les deux utiles pour comprendre pourquoi la correction ne peut pas être traitée automatiquement. D’une part, le système de feuille de temps indique que ce quart ne figure pas comme un quart vous appartenant, ce qui veut dire que l’identifiant du service ne correspond pas au dossier rattaché à votre identifiant employé E M P, deux neuf zéro, huit zéro deux. D’autre part, la vérification d’admissibilité de correction renvoie que la période de paie pour ce quart est déjà clôturée, et dans ce cas le système bloque toute soumission de correction même avant l’étape d’envoi. Je vous l’explique en détail parce qu’il y a ici deux causes possibles distinctes : soit la date ou l’heure de début du quart n’est pas exactement celle du service concerné, soit il s’agit bien du bon service mais la correction nécessite désormais un traitement manuel exceptionnel puisque la période est fermée. Comme je ne peux pas soumettre une correction bloquée ni modifier un quart qui n’apparaît pas comme le vôtre, la meilleure suite dépend de ce que vous préférez : soit nous revérifions ensemble la date et l’heure exactes du quart pour voir si un autre identifiant serait correct, soit je peux vous proposer un transfert vers un agent humain pour une prise en charge manuelle liée à une période de paie clôturée et à une possible discordance de quart. Poulez-vous me dire si vous voulez revérifier les détails du quart, ou si vous préférez que je vous transfère à un agent en expliquant déjà tout le contexte pour vous éviter de tout répéter ?

On garde ce quart-là, c’est le bon.  
J’ai besoin d’une correction de paie pour ce service.

Je comprends, et merci de le confirmer clairement, surtout si vous êtes certaine que ce quart est bien le bon. Dans ce cas, je dois être transparente avec vous : je ne peux pas soumettre moi-même la correction dans le système, parce que la vérification a renvoyé à la fois un quart non rattaché à votre dossier et une période de paie déjà clôturée, et ces deux éléments sont des blocages système, pas seulement un avertissement. Quand une période de paie est fermée, la demande automatique serait rejetée, et quand le quart n’apparaît pas comme vous appartenant, il y a aussi un risque de modifier le mauvais dossier, ce que la procédure m’interdit strictement. Comme vous maintenez que c’est bien le bon quart, cela ressemble à une situation qui nécessite soit une exception de traitement, soit une revue manuelle du dossier par un agent humain ayant la capacité d’enquêter sur l’affectation du quart et sur la paie clôturée. Je peux donc vous proposer un transfert vers un agent en résumant précisément que vous êtes authentifiée, que le quart concerné est le 27 mai 2026 à 7 heures du matin, que l’identifiant construit est S H F, 20260527, 0700, et que le système indique à la fois une discordance d’attribution et une période de paie fermée. Si vous êtes d’accord, je lance le transfert maintenant, et cela vous évitera de devoir répéter toutes les informations depuis le début.

per_turn_explanations.1: The assistant front-loads a lot of process explanation (identity check, pay-period eligibility, types of corrections, how to enter totals vs deltas) before learning the user’s specifics. It also asks for multiple data points “in one go,” which is heavy for voice and not necessary yet. This creates cognitive load and includes disproportionate background relative to the user’s simple request for help.
per_turn_explanations.2: While it correctly adapts to the user’s constraint (two items at a time), it still adds extra policy justification, examples of correction types, and a warning about rereading identifiers—more than needed at this moment. The core ask could be delivered in 1–2 sentences; as spoken, it’s longer than necessary but still understandable.
per_turn_explanations.3: The assistant confirms authentication and then explains the multi-step payroll workflow at length. It also repeats the employee’s name and spells/reads the ID again, which is not strictly necessary for the next step in a voice call. The final request (date + start time) is clear, but it’s buried under extra explanation, increasing cognitive load.
per_turn_explanations.4: Reading back the constructed shift identifier and asking for confirmation is appropriate for voice accuracy. However, it adds more rationale about internal policy and error risks than needed; the user likely only needs the ID and a simple confirmation prompt. Still, the structure is mostly digestible.
per_turn_explanations.5: The assistant reports two key results (shift not owned; pay period closed) but then over-explains with multiple causal hypotheses and process constraints, making the turn long for voice. It also offers two options with a lot of detail rather than a brief recommendation and a single clarifying question. This is information-dense and risks overwhelming the listener.
per_turn_explanations.6: The assistant reiterates the same blockers and constraints with substantial repetition, then proposes a transfer with a very detailed recap (including spelling/formatting of the shift ID again). A brief statement of inability + the single next step (transfer/escalation) would be more voice-appropriate. The level of detail is disproportionate given the user’s clear preference to proceed with the same shift.

conversation_trace.content: Bonjour, j’ai besoin d’aide pour une demande de prolongation d’une licence supervisée.

Bonjour, bien sûr, je peux vous aider avec cette demande de prolongation de licence supervisée, et je vais vous accompagner étape par étape pour que ce soit clair et conforme. Comme il s’agit d’une question de licence professionnelle, la politique exige une vérification prestataire avant que je puisse consulter le dossier ou lancer toute action, et je préfère vous expliquer cela maintenant pour éviter tout aller-retour ensuite. J’aurai donc besoin de trois éléments en une seule fois : votre numéro N P I à dix chiffres, votre code d’établissement principal, et votre code P I N à quatre chiffres. Après cela, je consulterai d’abord l’état actuel de votre licence, puis je vérifierai votre admissibilité à une prolongation, car les prolongations ne sont possibles que dans les soixante jours précédant l’expiration et jamais après expiration, et les durées autorisées sont exactement trente, soixante, ou quatre-vingt-dix jours. Comme vous avez déjà indiqué qu’il s’agit d’une prolongation supervisée, j’aurai ensuite aussi besoin du numéro N P I du médecin superviseur, qui doit être différent du vôtre, mais nous le confirmerons seulement après l’authentification et la revue du dossier.
Je préfère y aller par étapes, s’il vous plaît. On peut commencer juste par le N P I ?

Oui, absolument, on peut avancer calmement, et je comprends très bien que vous préfériez procéder étape par étape au téléphone. Je dois tout de même vous signaler que je ne pourrai pas lancer la vérification tant que je n’aurai pas les trois éléments requis ensemble, à savoir le numéro N P I, le code de votre établissement principal, et votre code P I N à quatre chiffres, parce que la politique d’authentification prestataire demande l’ensemble complet avant tout accès au dossier. Cela dit, nous pouvons commencer par le premier élément maintenant, puis enchaîner immédiatement avec les deux autres ensuite, ce qui permet de garder la conversation simple tout en respectant les règles de sécurité et de confidentialité. Une fois cette vérification terminée, je consulterai votre dossier de licence actuel, y compris la date d’expiration et tout détail d’extension existant, puis je vérifierai votre admissibilité avant de recueillir le N P I du superviseur et la durée choisie, qui devra être de trente, soixante, ou quatre-vingt-dix jours. Vous pouvez donc me donner votre numéro N P I maintenant, et juste après, merci de me donner aussi votre code d’établissement principal et votre code P I N à quatre chiffres pour que je puisse finaliser la vérification sans retard.
D’accord. Mon N P I est le trois deux deux cinq deux trois un sept deux quatre. Mon code établissement principal est E Y trait d’union trois huit L. Et mon code P I N est neuf cinq zéro un.

Merci, je récapitule ce que j’ai bien reçu et utilisé pour la vérification, afin d’éviter toute erreur sur des identifiants sensibles. J’ai authentifié le numéro N P I trois deux deux cinq deux trois un sept deux quatre, le code d’établissement principal E Y, trait d’union, trois huit, L, et le code P I N neuf cinq zéro un. La vérification a réussi, vous êtes bien authentifié, et le dossier correspond à Julien Vincent, avec l’identifiant employé E M P, quatre un huit, huit neuf sept. Comme l’authentification prestataire est maintenant complète, je peux passer à la consultation du dossier de licence, ce qui est obligatoire avant toute modification, parce que nous devons d’abord revoir l’état actuel de la licence et toute information d’extension déjà existante avant de vérifier l’admissibilité.
